progression.startsWith: Prepare matched water and oily samples. The video opens: Shake a little soap solution in pure water, and you get a tall froth. Shake the same soap in hard water, and it turns cloudy, and the froth barely forms. A detergent froths in both.

teaching.task: In soft water, soap and a detergent both froth. In hard water, soap turns cloudy and barely froths, while the detergent keeps going. How do you set up a fair comparison, measure what you see, and use the results to explain how soaps and detergents work?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the observation to explain (1); (2) the aim; hard water made with a known amount of CaCl₂ (chloride checked by an optional NaCl tube); six tubes including controls (2); (3) part A method: same volume, drops, shakes, time; the controls show water alone barely froths (3); (4) the variables (4); (5) results: soap fails in hard water, detergent barely changes (5); (6) cause: scum locks up soap; detergent's calcium salt stays dissolved (recall, 6); (7) part B: oil emulsion timing (7); (8) the emulsion is soap-coated oil droplets; less free soap in hard water, so the droplets join sooner; two tests agree (8); (9) reliability (9); (10) validity and accuracy (10); (11) hazards and controls (11); memory aid (12); attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: soap froths tall in pure water but turns cloudy and barely froths in hard water, while a detergent froths in both, so the practical asks how to show that fairly, measure it and explain it. Hard water is made from a known amount of calcium chloride in distilled water, with distilled water as the soft sample and a sodium chloride tube as a check on the added chloride. In part A each tube gets the same water volume and drops, is stoppered, shaken ten times and the froth height is measured after thirty seconds; the variables card names two independent variables, the cleaning agent and the water. The example results show soap losing most of its froth and forming white specks in hard water while the detergent barely changes. Recalling the soaps video, two soap ions bind each calcium ion as insoluble scum, so every locked soap particle is lost, while the detergent's calcium salt is much more soluble. Part B times how long shaken oil stays emulsified, because froth is not cleaning; soap particles coat the oil droplets and hard water leaves fewer free to do it, so both tests agree. Repeats, matched shaking and timing, a pure detergent and careful reading keep the results reliable, valid and accurate, and the risk table says low hazard, not no hazard. The memory aid is soap makes scum in hard water, detergents mostly don't. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Shake a little soap solution in pure water, and you get a tall froth. Shake the same soap in hard water, and it turns cloudy, and the froth barely forms. A detergent froths in both. Let's show that fairly, measure it, and explain it.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student added soap solution, one drop at a time, to 10 mL samples of water, stoppering and shaking after each drop, until a froth formed that lasted for 30 seconds. The table shows the results. | Sample | Drops of soap solution needed | Appearance | Distilled water | 2 | clear | Sample X | 3 | clear | Sample Y | 17 | cloudy, white solid | Explain the result for sample Y. Include a net ionic equation for one hardness ion (state which ion you use), using sodium stearate, C₁₇H₃₅COONa, as the soap." (3 marks.) Answer: sample Y is hard water: it contains Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺ ions; the stearate ions react with them to form an insoluble solid, the white scum: 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻(aq) + Ca²⁺(aq) → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca(s), or 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻(aq) + Mg²⁺(aq) → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Mg(s) (either earns the mark); the first drops (about 15 more than distilled water) are used up making scum, so lasting froth forms only once enough hardness ions have been removed for free soap to remain. Crossed mistake: "Sample Y contains more salt (sodium chloride)" (hardness is calcium and magnesium ions; sodium salts don't form scum with soap). (A2) "A student compared a soap with a dishwashing detergent in tap water from a hard-water area. She added 5 drops of soap solution to one test tube of the tap water and 10 drops of the dishwashing detergent to another, shook each tube, and found that the detergent produced more froth. She concluded that detergents work better than soaps in hard water. Explain why her conclusion is not valid, and describe TWO changes to her method that would make it valid." (4 marks.) Answer: two things changed besides the type of agent (drops: 5 against 10; and a commercial detergent may contain softeners or other ingredients), so the froth difference can't be put down to soap against detergent alone; also no soft-water comparison and no control; changes: a pure detergent (for example sodium dodecyl sulfate); test each agent in both soft (distilled) and hard water with the same number of drops, and compare each agent's hard-water result with its own soft-water result (Revision 3: no equal-strength comparison between the agents is needed or claimed); water-only controls; same shaking and timing. Crossed mistake: "Repeat the test three times and average" (repeats check reliability; the unequal drops are still there; s07).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the structure and action of soaps and detergents" "describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)" (carried by the risk table, route review change 5) this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the investigation; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: the aim; hard water made from a known amount of calcium chloride in distilled water (calcium proposed as the cause from its chemistry; an optional sodium chloride tube checks the added chloride) and distilled water as soft water; six tubes (soap or detergent or nothing, in soft or hard water); part A, the froth test (same volume, same drops, ten shakes, read the froth height after 30 s); the variables; the results and their cause, recalled in one pass; part B, the oil emulsion test in fresh tubes (add oil, shake, time until a clear oil layer reappears: how long the oil stays dispersed, not cleaning itself); why the two tests agree; reliability; validity and accuracy (hand shaking, unequal drops, commercial products with extra ingredients, reading the froth); the risk assessment and disposal. Recalled, not re-taught: the soap and detergent structures, micelles, emulsification, droplet repulsion, the scum equation, why detergent calcium salts stay dissolved (all chem-m7-c12); validity, reliability, accuracy, word, feature, fix (skills-s07, chem-m7-p03). Not here: saponification in the lab (c12 covers the reaction; making soap is not this route's practical); water softening by sodium carbonate or ion exchange; biodegradability tests; surface tension and the pepper demonstration (c12 Decisions); cationic and non-ionic detergents in the lab (named only on the c12 recall chip).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c12: oil yellow; the soap tail pale blue and head red with "−"; Na⁺ grey-amber; Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ teal; scum grey-white; plus the tube line-up colours (soap amber, detergent violet, water only grey; soft pale blue, hard teal); hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant, as chem-m7-p03 and p04): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the tube plates; the right third holds the current card (method step, variables, results, validity card, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends. Plates and owner rules: no people or hands (drops are added by coded dropper outlines, shaking is c12's coded rock of the tube plate, rotation only, and the froth is measured with a coded ruler overlay); real objects as painted plates, listed by filename, never stretched; particles and equations coded in the c12 style; at most about three bright text items; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (about 15 to 30 s) with one crossed-out mistake; original HSC-style questions only; real GHS classifications; school rules checked against NSW Chemical Safety in Schools (sources in "Safety facts check"); Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims; optional key notes hold. No human figures.
